paragraphs: This paper brings three image-analysis tasks into one probabilistic model: grouping similar images, dividing each image into objects, and associating words with those objects. It uses visual features and can also incorporate accompanying annotations when they are available. Connecting these tasks lets the model describe both the collection as a whole and the contents of individual images.

An important modeling assumption is that an object can contain a mixture of different visual components. Mixture models connect these components to object types, rather than requiring every object to have a uniform appearance. The model infers the number of image classes and object types, along with the feature mixtures, through a nonparametric Bayesian approach.

The authors also introduce a logistic stick-breaking process to form spatially contiguous objects, addressing the need for segments to occupy connected image regions. They use variational Bayesian inference for efficient computation and present examples from two image databases. The contribution is a unified way to connect collection-level organization, object segmentation, and localized words within the same analysis.
neurips-2009-a-bayesian-model-for-simult.tldr: A Bayesian model jointly groups images, segments objects, and links objects to words while inferring how many image classes and object types are needed.

paragraphs: Information gathering usually serves one of two purposes: improving a model during training or resolving uncertainty about a particular case during diagnosis. Training-time active learning selects data expected to improve classification, while diagnosis-time acquisition selects additional features of the current case. This paper develops a model and inference methods that connect those decisions.

Under the proposed framework, a diagnostic challenge can guide information gathering beyond the case currently being examined. A recommended sequence may include collecting new information about that case and acquiring information about cases already in the training collection. The training library therefore becomes part of the diagnostic decision process, rather than something treated as fixed once prediction begins.

This connection matters when information is costly and resources are scarce. The methods can guide expansion of a case library within a budget, but their broader contribution is a class of real-time diagnostic policies that considers both sources of information together. The stated advance is the decision framework itself: current diagnostic needs can help determine where further learning effort should go.
neurips-2009-breaking-boundaries-between.tldr: A unified information-gathering framework lets diagnostic decisions guide data collection for both the current case and the training library.

paragraphs: Decentralized control studies decision problems involving multiple agents that do not have complete information. The paper considers decentralized partially observable Markov decision processes and their equivalent game formulation. General versions have very high worst-case computational complexity, whether the agents cooperate or compete. This makes restricted models especially important for understanding when planning becomes more manageable.

Some earlier reductions in complexity rely on independence relationships within the model. Such assumptions remove particular dependencies from the decision problem. The paper examines how much those simplifications depend on preserving the assumptions precisely, rather than treating independence as an approximately satisfied property.

The central finding is that very small relaxations of the studied independence assumptions can restore the complexity of the general problem. Thus, the easier special cases have boundaries that can be computationally consequential. This is a worst-case result about classes of problems: it shows that the earlier complexity reductions do not necessarily extend to closely related models. Its significance is to clarify how narrowly some tractable or less difficult formulations must be interpreted.
neurips-2009-complexity-of-decentralized.tldr: Small relaxations of certain independence assumptions can make decentralized control as computationally difficult as the general case.

paragraphs: Range search asks for every database point whose dissimilarity to a query falls within a specified threshold. This operation supports methods such as local regression, density estimation, neighborhood graphs, and outlier detection. The paper develops an efficient search algorithm for situations where dissimilarity is measured by a Bregman divergence.

The difficulty is geometric. Many established search methods rely on the triangle inequality to reason about distances and organize spatial searches. Bregman divergences generally do not satisfy that inequality, so those methods cannot simply be carried over. The relevant family includes relative entropy, Mahalanobis distance, Itakura-Saito divergence, and several divergences between matrices.

The authors derive geometric properties that support search without depending on the usual metric argument. They combine these properties with a recently proposed decomposition of space for Bregman divergences. The abstract identifies this as the first range-search algorithm covering an arbitrary Bregman divergence. Its significance is to make efficient neighborhood retrieval available across a broad family of dissimilarity measures used in learning.
neurips-2009-efficient-bregman-range-sea.tldr: New geometric results enable efficient range search for arbitrary Bregman divergences despite their general lack of a triangle inequality.

paragraphs: This paper studies how relationships between tasks affect prediction in multi-task Gaussian process regression. Its setting is asymmetric: learning one primary task is the objective, while a secondary task supplies potentially useful information. The question is how the correlation between those tasks influences the primary task's prediction error and its improvement as data become available.

The authors derive bounds on the primary task's generalization error and learning curve. Their analysis connects the multi-task model to single-task Gaussian processes, providing a way to understand transfer through a more familiar setting. The emphasis is on characterizing the consequences of task relationships, rather than assuming that related observations automatically provide enough information for the primary problem.

They also examine a particularly specific case: inputs are one-dimensional, sampling is optimal, and observations come only from the secondary task. Under these conditions, the limitations of the multi-task approach can be quantified explicitly. This result gives a precise setting in which to assess what secondary-task data can accomplish when direct observations of the primary task are absent.
neurips-2009-generalization-errors-and-l.tldr: The paper bounds how task correlations affect Gaussian process transfer and explicitly quantifies its limitations in a restricted secondary-data-only setting.

paragraphs: Topic models serve two purposes: predicting text and giving people a topic-based representation of a document collection. Users often treat the inferred topics as meaningful summaries and use them to inspect a model or explore a corpus. This paper asks how to evaluate that human-facing role quantitatively, rather than assuming predictive success establishes interpretability.

The authors introduce measures of semantic meaning in inferred topics and support them with large-scale user studies. These measures assess aspects of the topic representation that earlier evaluations based on held-out likelihood fail to detect. Held-out likelihood evaluates how well a model predicts unseen text; the new evaluation addresses whether its topics convey meaning to people.

The key finding is that models with better held-out likelihood may produce less semantically meaningful topics. This is a possible divergence between two kinds of quality, not a claim that prediction and interpretability always conflict. For applications involving summaries or exploration, the result establishes why evaluating predictive fit alone can leave an important part of the model's usefulness unmeasured.
neurips-2009-reading-tea-leaves-how-huma.tldr: Human studies show that better text prediction does not necessarily produce topics that people find more meaningful.

paragraphs: This paper explores how other images with a similar overall description can help divide a scene into regions without supervised segmentation. Its central idea is that an input image can be explained using partial matches from multiple similar scenes. Different parts of the input can therefore draw support from different reference images.

The method uses a Markov random field formulation to optimize the segmentation over those matches while taking image boundaries into account. Matching and segmentation are connected: the selected correspondences help explain regions, while boundary information helps determine where regions should separate. This gives the method a way to combine evidence from similar scenes with evidence inside the input itself.

The resulting segments are then used to search a large image database again for better matches to individual target regions. Region discovery thus guides a more focused retrieval step. On data gathered from LabelMe, the authors report improved detection of occluding boundaries over previous methods. The stated finding supports the usefulness of partial scene matches and region-specific retrieval for locating those boundaries.
neurips-2009-segmenting-scenes-by-matchi.tldr: Combining partial matches from similar images with boundary-aware segmentation improves occluding-boundary detection on LabelMe data.

paragraphs: Collecting image labels from many people can help build large training databases, but their responses may differ in reliability. Some labelers have greater expertise, some provide noisy answers, and some may be adversarial. Images also differ in difficulty. Consequently, disagreement can reflect properties of both the people labeling an image and the image itself.

The paper introduces a probabilistic model that estimates three unknowns together: each image's label, each labeler's expertise, and each image's difficulty. Instead of treating every vote as equally informative, it interprets the observed labels through these interacting quantities. This is useful when expertise is not known beforehand and multiple responses must be combined into one estimated label.

On simulated and real data, the model outperforms majority voting and shows robustness to noisy and adversarial labelers. These are empirical findings from the reported evaluations. Their practical meaning is that accounting jointly for who supplied a label and how difficult the item is can improve label aggregation over simply choosing the most common answer.
neurips-2009-whose-vote-should-count-mor.tldr: Jointly estimating image labels, labeler expertise, and image difficulty improves on majority voting in simulated and real-data evaluations.

paragraphs: An interactive assistant may observe a person's actions without knowing the goal behind them. This paper formalizes that situation using hidden-goal Markov decision processes and studies the computational difficulty of choosing assistance. Even with deterministic dynamics, selecting an optimal action over a finite horizon is PSPACE-complete in this model.

The authors then introduce helper action MDPs, a more restricted formulation in which useful assistance is accepted and unhelpful assistance can be easily ignored. They identify classes with PSPACE-complete and NP-complete decision problems, as well as a class solvable in polynomial time. These distinctions show how the structure of the interaction affects computational difficulty.

The paper also gives guarantees for simple policies in general helper action MDPs. A myopic policy has regret relative to an assistant that knows the goal bounded by the entropy of the initial goal distribution. A variation has worst-case regret logarithmic in the number of goals for any goal distribution. These bounds connect the cost of uncertain assistance to uncertainty about what the person wants.
neurips-2010-a-computational-decision-th.tldr: The paper characterizes the complexity of assisting someone with a hidden goal and proves regret bounds for simple helper policies.

paragraphs: Related regression tasks may share some useful features without sharing all of them or assigning them similar weights. The paper explains why this matters for block regularization, which encourages shared feature structure. When overlap is too limited or shared coefficients are highly uneven, such methods can perform worse than fitting tasks with separate elementwise regularization.

The proposed approach divides the regression parameters into two components and applies different regularization to each. This lets the model accommodate a mixture of structures rather than requiring the entire parameter collection to fit one pattern. The motivating question is whether shared structure can help when present without imposing the same structural expectation everywhere.

The authors report theoretical and empirical improvements over both elementwise and block regularization across the full range of overlaps considered. They also establish guarantees under high-dimensional scaling, where the number of features grows with the number of observations. The contribution is a concrete demonstration that combining differently regularized components can handle partial sharing more effectively in the studied multiple-regression setting.
neurips-2010-a-dirty-model-for-multi-tas.tldr: Splitting regression parameters into differently regularized components improves multi-task learning across the studied range of feature sharing.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks to improve classification by choosing which examples should receive labels. This paper presents and analyzes an agnostic active learning algorithm that avoids maintaining a version space. A version space is a restricted collection of candidate classifiers that a learner keeps during training and from which it selects its eventual answer.

The distinction concerns how learning is organized. In the previous approaches described by the authors, retaining and updating that candidate set is a continuing requirement, and the returned classifier must belong to it. The proposed algorithm removes this requirement, shedding the computational work and brittleness associated with maintaining the restricted set throughout learning.

The analysis shows that removing the version-space mechanism still permits substantial improvements over supervised learning for classification. The result therefore separates the benefits of active learning from this particular way of implementing it. Its significance is that an algorithm can retain meaningful advantages from selective labeling without carrying the same candidate-set machinery that earlier approaches relied on.
neurips-2010-agnostic-active-learning-wi.tldr: An agnostic active learning algorithm avoids maintaining a restricted candidate set while still allowing substantial gains over supervised classification.

paragraphs: Isotonic regression fits predictions subject to ordering constraints. Large instances can involve many variables and an even larger collection of constraints, making the organization of the computation important. This paper introduces an algorithm that tackles the problem by recursively partitioning the solution space into smaller pieces.

For each partitioning step, the authors establish an equivalent network flow formulation and develop efficient methods for solving it. They prove that the resulting sequence of partitions converges to the global solution. The subdivision is therefore supported by a correctness result connecting the smaller problems to the original optimization objective.

The network flow problems can themselves be decomposed, providing another level of subdivision for very large instances. Simulated examples demonstrate both the predictive usefulness of isotonic regression and the algorithm's favorable computational behavior, including cases with 200,000 variables and 10 million constraints. The contribution combines a global convergence guarantee with a computational strategy demonstrated at substantial scale, rather than relying on partitioning solely as an informal shortcut.
neurips-2010-decomposing-isotonic-regres.tldr: Recursive partitioning and decomposable network flow problems enable large-scale isotonic regression with convergence to the global solution.

paragraphs: This paper extends a traditional sparse coding approach from a single flat layer to a two-layer representation. Its focus is how to organize coding hierarchically, so that a representation can have multiple levels. The proposed architecture begins with two layers and is designed to extend naturally to deeper structures.

The two-layer scheme is derived from a theoretical analysis of nonlinear function approximation. That analysis extends results for local coordinate coding and provides the basis for moving beyond the single-layer formulation. The role of theory here is to motivate the coding construction through its relationship to function approximation, giving the architectural extension an explicit mathematical foundation.

The authors also report improved performance on benchmark datasets using the deep coding approach. This empirical result accompanies the theoretical derivation, supporting the usefulness of the proposed representation in the evaluated settings. Together, the contributions connect a specific two-layer construction, a route to hierarchical multilayer coding, and observed improvements from using the resulting approach.
neurips-2010-deep-coding-network-43e9e1d.tldr: A theoretically derived two-layer sparse coding scheme extends to deeper hierarchies and improves performance on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Estimating a room's three-dimensional layout involves understanding both its surfaces and the objects within it. This paper identifies a gap in the approaches it discusses: they recover spatial layout without modeling the three-dimensional interaction between objects and that layout. The authors argue that this interaction supplies useful information for scene interpretation.

Their approach represents objects parametrically in three dimensions. This representation makes it possible to incorporate volumetric constraints from the physical world into the prediction process. Objects are therefore described in terms that allow reasoning about the space they occupy and their relationship to the surrounding layout, bringing object geometry into the room-estimation problem.

The authors add this volumetric reasoning to existing structured prediction techniques and report a significant improvement over the state of the art. The finding supports the value of modeling objects and surfaces together when estimating spatial layout. The main contribution is the use of an explicit three-dimensional object representation to make physical constraints available to the prediction method.
neurips-2010-estimating-spatial-layout-o.tldr: Adding volumetric constraints through parametric 3D object representations significantly improves room-layout estimation in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: When the brain estimates one property of a stimulus, variation in other stimulus properties can act as noise. This paper studies that effect for binocular disparity, a cue used in depth inference. It analyzes a binocular energy model responding to random dot stereograms and finds response variability substantially different from the commonly assumed Poisson-like noise.

The authors calculate the Fisher information about disparity in the model's monocular inputs. This gives an upper bound on how much information a model could extract from those inputs. They then examine how much information is lost when different combinations of the inputs produce a single scalar neuronal response.

For typical spike counts in the studied depth-inference setting, monocular stimulus variability limits available information more than intrinsic neuronal noise. The standard position-disparity model produces the largest information loss, while phase-disparity neurons preserve more input information. The abstract associates the former with common neurons in monkey primary visual cortex and the latter primarily with higher cortical regions. The findings emphasize that evaluating a neural code requires accounting for stimulus variability as well as internal noise.
neurips-2010-evaluating-neuronal-codes-f.tldr: In the studied binocular-depth setting, stimulus variability limits information more than intrinsic noise at typical spike counts, with losses depending on neuronal response type.

paragraphs: Gaussian graphical models describe relationships through the structure of an inverse covariance matrix. Recovering a sparse graph requires choosing which connections to retain. This paper studies an extended Bayesian information criterion as a selection objective, usable either when searching across graphs or when choosing a tuning parameter for methods such as the graphical lasso.

The authors establish asymptotic consistency in a setting where both the number of variables and the sample size increase. Their treatment also permits the number of nonzero parameters in the true model to grow. That allowance matters because connected graphs require increasing numbers of connections as their number of variables grows.

In simulations, the criterion is combined with the graphical lasso and compared with cross-validation and ordinary Bayesian information criterion. It performs better in the studied setting where both the variable count and the number of nonzero parameters scale with sample size. The theoretical and empirical contributions therefore address model selection when the underlying graph can become larger and more complex as more data arrive.
neurips-2010-extended-bayesian-informati.tldr: An extended Bayesian information criterion has consistency guarantees and favorable simulation results for Gaussian graph selection as model size grows.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification depends on how similarity is measured around each example. This paper learns a local distance metric using information from parametric generative models of the classes. Whereas conventional approaches described in the abstract learn metrics through class separation alone, this method also uses a model of how class data are distributed.

The analysis focuses on bias in an information-theoretic error quantity caused by having finitely many samples. Using knowledge supplied by the generative models, the authors choose a local metric that maximally reduces that bias. This connects the choice of neighborhood geometry to a specific sampling effect, rather than treating distance learning only as a direct separation problem.

The asymptotic analysis also reveals a relationship between metric learning and dimensionality reduction. Empirical experiments show improved nearest-neighbor classification on several datasets using simple class-conditional generative models. The reported results demonstrate that even these simple distributional models can provide useful information for shaping local distances and improving the final discriminative prediction.
neurips-2010-generative-local-metric-lea.tldr: Generative class models guide local distance learning to reduce finite-sample bias and improve nearest-neighbor classification in experiments.

paragraphs: Classification becomes expensive at prediction time when a system must consider a very large number of possible classes. Testing every class can become computationally impractical. This paper tackles that cost by learning structure over the labels, using both a tree of classifiers and a low-dimensional representation of labels.

The tree-learning algorithm optimizes the loss of the overall tree, and the authors report better accuracy than existing tree labeling methods. Separately, their label-embedding method represents labels in a lower-dimensional space. It is faster than approaches without embeddings and more accurate than existing embedding approaches in the reported comparisons.

The final method combines the two ideas into a label embedding tree. The authors report that it outperforms alternatives, including One-vs-Rest, while making predictions orders of magnitude faster. The contribution is therefore both computational and predictive: organizing a large label set and compressing its representation can work together to reduce test-time cost while improving accuracy in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2010-label-embedding-trees-for-l.tldr: Combining learned classifier trees with label embeddings improves accuracy and delivers orders-of-magnitude prediction speedups in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning shares information across related prediction problems. The paper identifies a restriction in a prominent multi-task support vector machine formulation: its class-specific weight vectors require the tasks to use the same class set. This can constrain how related problems are combined when their prediction categories differ.

The authors instead extend large margin nearest-neighbor learning to the multi-task setting. Predictions rely on the nearest-neighbor rule rather than a collection of separating hyperplanes. Because this decision rule naturally handles multiple classes, the formulation offers a way to share learning across tasks without organizing the model around the same class-specific construction.

The resulting method is evaluated on real-world insurance data and speech classification problems. It consistently outperforms single-task nearest-neighbor methods using several metrics and the state-of-the-art multi-task classifiers included in those evaluations. The findings support learning a shared approach to distance and neighborhood structure as a useful basis for multi-task prediction, especially in addressing the class-set restriction motivating the work.
neurips-2010-large-margin-multi-task-met.tldr: Extending large margin nearest-neighbor learning across tasks improves insurance and speech classification in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning selects a kernel while training a support vector machine. This paper argues that relying on the classification margin alone creates scaling and initialization problems in many existing approaches. A margin can change with the scale of the representation, so its size by itself does not adequately characterize kernel quality.

The authors instead evaluate the margin relative to the radius of the minimum ball enclosing the data and develop a corresponding minimization formulation. The objective is invariant to scaling the learned kernel. For linear combinations of basis kernels, it is also invariant to scaling those basis kernels and to the choice of norm constraint on the combination coefficients.

The paper establishes differentiability of the formulation and proposes a gradient projection algorithm to optimize it. Experiments report significant improvements over an SVM using a uniform kernel combination and other state-of-the-art multiple kernel learning approaches. The contribution connects a scale-aware geometric criterion to an optimization method and demonstrates its empirical usefulness in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2010-learning-kernels-with-radiu.tldr: A margin-to-radius kernel criterion removes specified scaling sensitivities and improves on competing kernel-learning methods in experiments.

paragraphs: Estimating how much information a group of neurons carries depends strongly on correlations in their response variability. Measuring all such noise correlations becomes difficult because the number of pairwise parameters grows quadratically with population size. This paper proposes a parametric model for filling in missing correlation information.

The main assumption is that shared inputs give rise to noise correlations. On average, these correlations should therefore reflect signal correlations, which can be measured in neural populations. The authors specify a parametric relationship between the two and use an iterative procedure involving the Wishart distribution to complete the noise correlation matrix while working with positive definite matrices.

They apply the method to recordings from monkeys' primary somatosensory cortex during a two-alternative forced-choice task. They compare discrimination thresholds read out from the recorded population with the monkey's behavioral threshold. The method predicts different results from simpler schemes based on average noise correlations. This demonstrates that the structure used to complete missing correlations can materially affect conclusions about population information.
neurips-2010-linear-readout-from-a-neura.tldr: A model relating signal and noise correlations fills missing neural correlation data and yields different population-readout predictions from average-correlation schemes.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a theoretical connection between traditional perceptron algorithms and herding algorithms. It shows that both can be understood through the perceptron cycling theorem. Placing them within the same mathematical framework strengthens some existing results for herding and provides a basis for developing additional algorithms.

The connection suggests supervised forms of herding that make predictions conditional on input attributes. This brings herding into a prediction setting where the output depends on the observed example, as it does in conditional random fields and discriminative restricted Boltzmann machines. The authors develop and investigate several variants of this conditional approach.

The resulting algorithms perform better than or comparably to related classifiers, including the voted perceptron and discriminative restricted Boltzmann machine, in the reported investigation. The findings give the theoretical link a practical consequence: it supports a route from a shared theorem to useful supervised prediction methods. The contribution combines stronger understanding of herding with evidence that its conditional variants can compete with established classifiers.
neurips-2010-on-herding-and-the-perceptr.tldr: A shared connection to the perceptron cycling theorem strengthens herding theory and leads to competitive conditional herding classifiers.

paragraphs: Outliers can receive very large loss values during training and strongly influence the resulting predictor. One natural response is to cap the loss above a threshold. This paper studies how to retain the robustness associated with that idea while addressing the optimization difficulties often linked to robust, nonconvex losses.

The authors develop a relaxation of loss clipping that is globally solvable and can be applied to any standard loss function. The distinction between clipping and its relaxation is central: the global solvability claim belongs to the reformulated training method. The paper also states a robustness guarantee against outliers for this approach.

A generic procedure makes the construction applicable across standard training losses, and the authors demonstrate improved robustness in both regression and classification problems. The contribution is to connect outlier resistance with a practically solvable global training formulation. It shows that the computational difficulties associated with an initial robust-loss expression need not determine the possibilities available after the training problem is reformulated.
neurips-2010-relaxed-clipping-a-global-t.tldr: A globally solvable relaxation of loss clipping provides outlier robustness and improves robustness in regression and classification demonstrations.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks share weights across positions, reducing the number of parameters and building translation-related invariance into the architecture. This paper asks how a network can learn more complex invariances while retaining much of that parameter efficiency. Its answer is a modified pattern of weight sharing called a tiled convolutional network.

In the tiled pattern, neighboring hidden units need not use identical weights. Instead, weight sharing repeats between units separated by a fixed number of steps. Pooling across neighboring units then allows the architecture to learn invariances such as those associated with changes in scale or rotation. The network preserves regular sharing without requiring the same local weights at every adjacent position.

The authors provide an efficient learning algorithm based on Topographic ICA. They report highly competitive results on NORB and CIFAR-10 using the learned invariant features. The contribution is an architectural compromise: more flexibility in nearby feature detectors, together with repeated weights that retain many of the learning and scalability advantages of conventional convolutional networks.
neurips-2010-tiled-convolutional-neural-.tldr: Tiled weight sharing lets convolutional networks learn complex invariances while retaining parameter efficiency and achieving competitive benchmark results.

paragraphs: This paper treats classification with incomplete information as a matrix completion problem. The matrix contains feature and label entries, some of which are missing. Assuming that the underlying matrix has low rank lets the method address multiple labels per item, unspecified labels in a transductive setting, and missing feature values within one formulation.

The low-rank assumption ties the completion of these different entries together. The method also permits different loss functions for features and labels, allowing the optimization to treat those two kinds of observations differently. It formulates the task through nuclear norm minimization and solves it using a modified fixed-point continuation method with a guarantee of reaching the global optimum.

Results on several real-world tasks are described as satisfactory, suggesting that the low-rank assumption may be useful beyond narrowly structured examples. That empirical conclusion remains qualified: the results suggest the assumption is less restrictive than it might appear. The main contribution is a common optimization framework for three forms of incomplete or multiple-output data.
neurips-2010-transduction-with-matrix-co.tldr: Low-rank matrix completion jointly handles multiple labels, unspecified labels, and missing features through an optimization method with a global-optimum guarantee.
